drills.title: Lesson 1 · Foundations
drills.blurb: Objects, words, sentences, propositions, and the four kinds of sentences.

items.prompt:
What kind of sentence?

“The train arrives at noon.”
items.explain: It states a fact, so it is declarative.

items.prompt:
What kind of sentence?

“Where did you put my shoes?”
items.explain: It asks a question, so it is interrogative.

items.prompt:
What kind of sentence?

“Please close the window.”
items.explain: It gives a request or command, so it is imperative.

items.prompt:
What kind of sentence?

“What a beautiful sunset!”
items.explain: It shows strong feeling, so it is exclamatory.

items.prompt:
What kind of sentence?

“Dogs bark at strangers.”
items.explain: It states a fact, so it is declarative.

items.prompt:
What kind of sentence?

“How many apples are left?”
items.explain: It asks a question, so it is interrogative.

items.prompt:
What kind of sentence?

“Hand me the wrench.”
items.explain: It gives a command, so it is imperative.

items.prompt:
What kind of sentence?

“Wow, we won the game!”
items.explain: It bursts out with feeling, so it is exclamatory.

items.prompt:
What kind of sentence?

“The library opens early on Mondays.”
items.explain: It states a fact, so it is declarative.

items.prompt:
What kind of sentence?

“Are you coming with us?”
items.explain: It asks a question, so it is interrogative.

items.prompt:
What kind of sentence?

“Turn off the lights before you leave.”
items.explain: It tells someone to do something, so it is imperative.

items.prompt:
What kind of sentence?

“How cold this water is!”
items.explain: It expresses strong feeling, so it is exclamatory.

items.prompt:
What kind of sentence?

“My cousin plays the violin.”
items.explain: It states a fact, so it is declarative.

items.prompt:
What kind of sentence?

“Did the mail come yet?”
items.explain: It asks a question, so it is interrogative.

items.prompt:
What kind of sentence?

“Open your books to page ten.”
items.explain: It gives a command, so it is imperative.

items.prompt:
Is this a complete sentence?

“The children built a sandcastle.”
items.explain: It has a subject and a predicate and makes complete sense.

items.prompt:
Is this a complete sentence?

“running through the tall grass”
items.explain: No subject and no complete sense — it is only a fragment.

items.prompt:
Is this a complete sentence?

“Rain fell all night.”
items.explain: It makes complete sense: rain (subject) fell (predicate).

items.prompt:
Is this a complete sentence?

“after the long, tiring journey”
items.explain: It does not make complete sense on its own — a fragment.

items.prompt:
Is this a complete sentence?

“She plays soccer on Saturdays.”
items.explain: Subject (she) + predicate (plays) making complete sense.

items.prompt:
Is this a complete sentence?

“the bright red bicycle in the yard”
items.explain: There is no predicate — nothing is said about the bicycle.

items.prompt:
Is this a complete sentence?

“Birds fly south in winter.”
items.explain: It expresses a complete thought.

items.prompt:
Is this a complete sentence?

“when the storm finally passed”
items.explain: It leaves the thought unfinished — a fragment (a clause, not a sentence).

items.prompt:
Does this sentence express a proposition — something that is true or false?

“Water boils when it is heated.”
items.explain: It states something that can be judged true or false.

items.prompt:
Does this sentence express a proposition — something that is true or false?

“Close the door.”
items.explain: A command asserts nothing true or false, so it expresses no proposition.

items.prompt:
Does this sentence express a proposition — something that is true or false?

“Is the sky blue?”
items.explain: A question asserts nothing true or false, so it expresses no proposition.

items.prompt:
Does this sentence express a proposition — something that is true or false?

“Gold is a metal.”
items.explain: It states something that is true or false — a proposition.

items.prompt:
Does this sentence express a proposition — something that is true or false?

“What a mess this is!”
items.explain: An exclamation expresses feeling, not a statement judged true or false.

items.prompt:
Does this sentence express a proposition — something that is true or false?

“The moon circles the earth.”
items.explain: It makes a statement that is true or false.

items.prompt:
Does this sentence express a proposition — something that is true or false?

“Please be quiet.”
items.explain: A request asserts nothing true or false.

items.prompt:
Does this sentence express a proposition — something that is true or false?

“Whales are mammals.”
items.explain: A declarative statement — true or false — so it expresses a proposition.

items.prompt:
Which sense do we use to perceive this?

rolling thunder
items.explain: Thunder is a sound — we hear it.

items.prompt:
Which sense do we use to perceive this?

a rainbow
items.explain: A rainbow is seen — the sense of sight.

items.prompt:
Which sense do we use to perceive this?

honey on the tongue
items.explain: Sweetness is perceived by taste.

items.prompt:
Which sense do we use to perceive this?

bread baking in the oven
items.explain: The aroma is perceived by smell.

items.prompt:
Which sense do we use to perceive this?

a rough stone
items.explain: Roughness is felt — the sense of touch.

items.prompt:
Which sense do we use to perceive this?

a ringing bell
items.explain: A ring is a sound — we hear it.

items.prompt:
Which sense do we use to perceive this?

a sour lemon
items.explain: Sourness is perceived by taste.

items.prompt:
Which sense do we use to perceive this?

a warm blanket
items.explain: Warmth is felt — the sense of touch.

items.prompt:
Does this sentence need quotation marks around someone’s exact words?

Ben said, I finished my homework.
items.explain: “I finished my homework” are Ben’s exact words, so they take quotation marks.

items.prompt:
Does this sentence need quotation marks around someone’s exact words?

Ben said that he had finished his homework.
items.explain: This only reports what Ben said — no exact words, so no quotation marks.

items.prompt:
Does this sentence need quotation marks around someone’s exact words?

The captain shouted, Abandon ship!
items.explain: “Abandon ship!” are the captain’s exact words — quotation marks are needed.

items.prompt:
Does this sentence need quotation marks around someone’s exact words?

The captain ordered the crew to abandon ship.
items.explain: It reports the order rather than quoting exact words — no quotation marks.

items.prompt:
Does this sentence need quotation marks around someone’s exact words?

Mother asked, Have you fed the dog?
items.explain: Mother’s exact question takes quotation marks.

items.prompt:
Does this sentence need quotation marks around someone’s exact words?

Mother asked whether we had fed the dog.
items.explain: This reports the question indirectly — no exact words, so no quotation marks.

drills.title: Lesson 2 · The Noun
drills.blurb: Common & proper nouns, plurals, abbreviations, contractions, and sentence parts.

items.prompt:
Common or proper noun?

river
items.explain: “river” names any river, so it is common.

items.prompt:
Common or proper noun?

London
items.explain: “London” names one particular city, so it is proper.

items.prompt:
Common or proper noun?

teacher
items.explain: “teacher” fits any teacher, so it is common.

items.prompt:
Common or proper noun?

Mount Everest
items.explain: It names one particular mountain, so it is proper.

items.prompt:
Common or proper noun?

mountain
items.explain: “mountain” names any mountain, so it is common.

items.prompt:
Common or proper noun?

January
items.explain: A particular month’s name is proper (and capitalized).

items.prompt:
Common or proper noun?

dog
items.explain: “dog” fits any dog, so it is common.

items.prompt:
Common or proper noun?

Rover
items.explain: A particular dog’s name is proper.

items.prompt:
Common or proper noun?

city
items.explain: “city” names any city, so it is common.

items.prompt:
Common or proper noun?

Atlantic Ocean
items.explain: It names one particular ocean, so it is proper.

items.prompt: Which is the correct plural of “leaf”?
items.explain: An f often changes to ves: leaf → leaves.

items.prompt: Which is the correct plural of “baby”?
items.explain: y after a consonant → ies: baby → babies.

items.prompt: Which is the correct plural of “box”?
items.explain: After x, add es: box → boxes.

items.prompt: Which is the correct plural of “man”?
items.explain: “man” is irregular: man → men.

items.prompt: Which is the correct plural of “tooth”?
items.explain: “tooth” is irregular: tooth → teeth.

items.prompt: Which is the correct plural of “potato”?
items.explain: o after a consonant → oes: potato → potatoes.

items.prompt: Which is the correct plural of “key”?
items.explain: y after a vowel just adds s: key → keys.

items.prompt: Which is the correct plural of “wolf”?
items.explain: f changes to ves: wolf → wolves.

items.prompt: Which is the correct plural of “child”?
items.explain: “child” is irregular: child → children.

items.prompt: Which is the correct plural of “city”?
items.explain: y after a consonant → ies: city → cities.

items.prompt: What does the abbreviation “Dr.” stand for?
items.explain: “Dr.” is short for Doctor.

items.prompt: Which is the correct abbreviation for “Mister”?
items.explain: “Mister” is abbreviated Mr.

items.prompt: What does the abbreviation “Ave.” stand for?
items.explain: “Ave.” is short for Avenue.

items.prompt: What does the abbreviation “Jr.” stand for?
items.explain: “Jr.” is short for Junior.

items.prompt: What does the abbreviation “Mt.” stand for?
items.explain: “Mt.” is short for Mount (as in Mt. Everest).

items.prompt: Which is the correct abbreviation for “Professor”?
items.explain: “Professor” is abbreviated Prof.

items.prompt: What does the abbreviation “Dec.” stand for?
items.explain: “Dec.” is short for December.

items.prompt: What two words does “can’t” stand for?
items.explain: “can’t” = can + not.

items.prompt: What two words does “won’t” stand for?
items.explain: “won’t” = will not.

items.prompt: What two words does “they’re” stand for?
items.explain: “they’re” = they are.

items.prompt: What two words does “I’m” stand for?
items.explain: “I’m” = I am.

items.prompt: What two words does “isn’t” stand for?
items.explain: “isn’t” = is not.

items.prompt: What two words does “let’s” stand for?
items.explain: “let’s” = let us.

items.prompt: What two words does “we’ve” stand for?
items.explain: “we’ve” = we have.

items.prompt:
What is the simple subject?

“Horses gallop swiftly.”
items.explain: The sentence is about the horses — “Horses” is the subject.

items.prompt:
What is the predicate (the verb)?

“Children play outside.”
items.explain: “play” tells what the children do — it is the predicate.

items.prompt:
What is the copula (the linking verb)?

“Snow is white.”
items.explain: “is” links the subject to the predicate — it is the copula.

items.prompt:
What is the simple subject?

“The old clock stopped.”
items.explain: The bare subject is “clock” (the modifiers “The old” are not the simple subject).

items.prompt:
What is the predicate (the verb)?

“Rivers flow to the sea.”
items.explain: “flow” tells what the rivers do — it is the predicate.

items.prompt:
What is the copula (the linking verb)?

“The soup was hot.”
items.explain: “was” links the subject to the predicate — it is the copula.

drills.title: Lesson 3 · The Verb
drills.blurb: Finding verbs; action/being/state; transitive, intransitive & copulative; verb mistakes.

items.prompt:
Which word is the verb?

“Birds fly south.”
items.explain: “fly” tells what the birds do — it is the verb.

items.prompt:
Which word is the verb?

“The baby sleeps.”
items.explain: “sleeps” is the verb — it tells what the baby does.

items.prompt:
Which word is the verb?

“Farmers grow wheat.”
items.explain: “grow” tells what the farmers do.

items.prompt:
Which word is the verb?

“She sings sweetly.”
items.explain: “sings” is the action word — the verb.

items.prompt:
Which word is the verb?

“We are happy.”
items.explain: “are” is the verb (a being verb).

items.prompt:
Which word is the verb?

“The dog chased the cat.”
items.explain: “chased” tells the action — the verb.

items.prompt:
Which word is the verb?

“Snow melts in spring.”
items.explain: “melts” is the verb.

items.prompt:
Which word is the verb?

“They built a treehouse.”
items.explain: “built” tells what they did — the verb.

items.prompt:
Does this verb express action, being, or state?

“George runs.”
items.explain: “runs” is something done — action.

items.prompt:
Does this verb express action, being, or state?

“I am.”
items.explain: “am” expresses being.

items.prompt:
Does this verb express action, being, or state?

“The rocket launched.”
items.explain: “launched” is an action.

items.prompt:
Does this verb express action, being, or state?

“They are students.”
items.explain: “are” expresses being.

items.prompt:
Does this verb express action, being, or state?

“The house belongs to us.”
items.explain: “belongs” names a condition, not a deed — state.

items.prompt:
Does this verb express action, being, or state?

“Water freezes.”
items.explain: “freezes” is a change that happens — action.

items.prompt:
Is the verb transitive, intransitive, or copulative?

“Columbus discovered America.”
items.explain: “discovered” takes an object (America), so it is transitive.

items.prompt:
Is the verb transitive, intransitive, or copulative?

“Horses run.”
items.explain: “run” needs no object, so it is intransitive.

items.prompt:
Is the verb transitive, intransitive, or copulative?

“The soup tastes good.”
items.explain: “tastes” links “soup” to “good” — copulative.

items.prompt:
Is the verb transitive, intransitive, or copulative?

“She wrote a letter.”
items.explain: “wrote” takes an object (a letter) — transitive.

items.prompt:
Is the verb transitive, intransitive, or copulative?

“The baby smiled.”
items.explain: “smiled” needs no object — intransitive.

items.prompt:
Is the verb transitive, intransitive, or copulative?

“He is a doctor.”
items.explain: “is” links “He” to “doctor” — copulative.

items.prompt:
Is the verb transitive, intransitive, or copulative?

“Farmers plant corn.”
items.explain: “plant” takes an object (corn) — transitive.

items.prompt:
Is the verb transitive, intransitive, or copulative?

“The sun shines.”
items.explain: “shines” needs no object — intransitive.

items.prompt:
Is the verb transitive, intransitive, or copulative?

“The weather grew cold.”
items.explain: “grew” links “weather” to “cold” — copulative.

items.prompt:
Is the verb transitive, intransitive, or copulative?

“Dogs chase cars.”
items.explain: “chase” takes an object (cars) — transitive.

items.prompt:

Choose the correct verb:

Choose the correct verb:

“You ___ there when it happened.”

“Rivers flow to the sea.”

Which word is the verb?

“The clock ticks.”

Which word is the verb?

“Lightning flashed brightly.”

items.prompt:
Which word is the verb?

“Bees buzz softly.”
items.explain: “buzz” tells what the bees do — the verb.

Does this verb express action, being, or state?

“Snow falls.”

Does this verb express action, being, or state?

“They are ready.”

Does this verb express action, being, or state?

“The gate remains open.”

Choose the correct verb:

Choose the correct verb:

drills.title: Lesson 4 · Adjectives & Participles
drills.blurb: Adjectives, the two kinds, a/an, participles, and participial nouns.

items.prompt:
Which word is the adjective?

“The red ball bounced.”
items.explain: “red” describes the noun “ball” — it is the adjective.

items.prompt:
Which word is the adjective?

“A brave soldier marched.”
items.explain: “brave” describes the soldier.

items.prompt:
Which word is the adjective?

“She wore a silk dress.”
items.explain: “silk” describes the dress.

items.prompt:
Which word is the adjective?

“Three cats napped.”
items.explain: “Three” tells how many — a (definitive) adjective.

items.prompt:
Which word is the adjective?

“He told a funny story.”
items.explain: “funny” describes the story.

items.prompt:
Which word is the adjective?

“Cold water refreshes.”
items.explain: “Cold” describes the water.

items.prompt:
Which word is the adjective?

“The tall tree swayed.”
items.explain: “tall” describes the tree.

items.prompt:
Which word is the adjective?

“A wise owl watched.”
items.explain: “wise” describes the owl.

items.prompt:
Descriptive or definitive adjective?

ripe
items.explain: “ripe” names a quality, so it is descriptive.

items.prompt:
Descriptive or definitive adjective?

four
items.explain: “four” counts, giving no quality, so it is definitive.

items.prompt:
Descriptive or definitive adjective?

golden
items.explain: “golden” names a quality — descriptive.

items.prompt:
Descriptive or definitive adjective?

those
items.explain: “those” points out without a quality — definitive.

items.prompt:
Descriptive or definitive adjective?

gentle
items.explain: “gentle” names a quality — descriptive.

items.prompt:
Descriptive or definitive adjective?

many
items.explain: “many” tells amount without a quality — definitive.

items.prompt:
Descriptive or definitive adjective?

cheerful
items.explain: “cheerful” names a quality — descriptive.

items.prompt:
Descriptive or definitive adjective?

each
items.explain: “each” points out without a quality — definitive.

___ apple

___ hour

Choose a or an:

___ honest judge

Choose a or an:

___ elephant

Which participle is it — present, perfect, or compound?

“The laughing child ran off.”
items.explain: “laughing” ends in -ing and shows action going on — present.

Which participle is it — present, perfect, or compound?

“The broken vase lay there.”

items.prompt:
Which participle is it — present, perfect, or compound?

“Having finished, she left.”

items.prompt:
Which participle is it — present, perfect, or compound?

“the twinkling stars”

items.prompt:
Which participle is it — present, perfect, or compound?

“a written note”

items.prompt:
Which participle is it — present, perfect, or compound?

“Having eaten, they rested.”
items.explain: “Having eaten” uses “having” — compound.

Is the -ing word a participle or a participial noun?

“I enjoy swimming.”

Is the -ing word a participle or a participial noun?

“The swimming fish darted.”

items.prompt:
Is the -ing word a participle or a participial noun?

“Reading is fun.”

items.prompt:
Is the -ing word a participle or a participial noun?

“The barking dog woke us.”
items.explain: “barking” describes the dog (the dog barks) — a participle.

drills.title: Lesson 5 · The Pronoun
drills.blurb: Personal & possessive pronouns, the three persons, possessives & apostrophes, and appositives.

items.prompt:
Which word is the pronoun?

“She lost the book.”
items.explain: “She” stands in place of a noun — it is the pronoun.

items.prompt:
Which word is the pronoun?

“Farmers sold it.”
items.explain: “it” stands for a noun — the pronoun.

items.prompt:
Which word is the pronoun?

“They sailed away.”
items.explain: “They” stands in place of a noun — the pronoun.

items.prompt:
Which word is the pronoun?

“Tom likes them.”
items.explain: “them” stands for a noun — the pronoun.

items.prompt:
Which word is the pronoun?

“Did you call?”
items.explain: “you” stands for the person spoken to — the pronoun.

items.prompt:
Which word is the pronoun?

“It rained hard.”
items.explain: “It” stands in place of a noun — the pronoun.

items.prompt:
Which word is the pronoun?

“Grandma saw him.”
items.explain: “him” stands for a noun — the pronoun.

items.prompt:
Which word is the pronoun?

“I won the race.”
items.explain: “I” stands for the speaker — the pronoun.

items.prompt:
Which person is this pronoun?

“I”
items.explain: “I” is the speaker — first person.

items.prompt:
Which person is this pronoun?

“you”
items.explain: “you” is the one spoken to — second person.

items.prompt:
Which person is this pronoun?

“he”
items.explain: “he” is the one spoken of — third person.

items.prompt:
Which person is this pronoun?

“we”
items.explain: “we” includes the speaker — first person.

items.prompt:
Which person is this pronoun?

“they”
items.explain: “they” are the ones spoken of — third person.

items.prompt:
Which person is this pronoun?

“she”
items.explain: “she” is the one spoken of — third person.

items.prompt:
Which person is this pronoun?

“it”
items.explain: “it” is the thing spoken of — third person.

items.prompt:
Which person is this pronoun?

“thou” (old form)
items.explain: “thou” is an older word for the one spoken to — second person.

items.prompt:
Which is the correct possessive?

the hat of John

items.prompt:
Which is the correct possessive?

the horn of the ox

items.prompt:
Which is the correct possessive?

the shoes of the children

items.prompt:
Which is the correct possessive?

the car of the ladies

items.prompt:
Which is the correct possessive?

the coats of the boys
items.explain: More than one, ending in s — add just the apostrophe: the boys’ coats.

items.prompt:
Which is the correct possessive?

the shoes of the women
items.explain: “women” does not end in s, so add ’s: the women’s shoes.

items.prompt:
Which is the correct possessive?

the den of the fox
items.explain: One owner — add ’s: the fox’s den.

items.prompt:
Which is the correct possessive?

the nest of the birds (more than one)
